_comment: Polynesian expansion batch 163 - W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific (1876): ch. 1 (Myths of Creation - Vari's six children), ch. 4 (Exploits of Maui - the fire-god's secret), ch. 8 (Hades; or, The Doctrine of Spirit-world), ch. 9 (Veetini; or, the Immortality of the Soul). Tradition: Mangaia, Hervey (Cook) Islands. Topics 1 creation, 3 heroic, 7 cosmology. All passages are labeled paraphrase; existing records cover vatea-creation, maui-sun-captive, ina-fairy-voyager.

title.en: Vari, the Very Beginning, and Her Six Children

region.en: The hollow of Avaiki, Mangaia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 曼加亞阿瓦伊基之殼（象徵性定位）

source.work: W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 1, The Beginning of all Things (London 1876)

summary.en: The universe is the hollow of a vast coconut shell: at the tapering point three stationary root-spirits - the Root of all Existence, Breathing, and the Long-lived; in the narrow bottom the Great Mother Vari-ma-te-takere, knees and chin touching. From bits of her own sides she tears six children: Vatea the moon, half man half fish; Tinirau, Innumerable, lord of fish at the Sacred Isle; Tango at the Land of Red Parrot-feathers; Echo in the Hollow Grey Rocks; Raka, who keeps the bag of winds, his children blowing through holes at the horizon; and Tu-metua, who stays with her in the Mute Land where only signs speak.
summary.zh: 宇宙乃一大椰殼之中空：尖端處三位恆住根靈——萬有之根、呼吸者、長壽者；殼底窄處住大母瓦里馬特塔克雷，膝顎相觸。她自體側撕下六子：瓦特亞——半月半魚之月神；蒂尼勞——『無數者』，聖島魚群之主；坦戈居紅鸚鵡羽之地；回聲居灰巖空洞；拉卡掌風袋，其子女即各路旋風，各自據地平線之風口吹拂；幼子圖梅圖阿則留侍慈母於『無言之鄉』——彼處唯以眉眼作語。

sensitivity.note: Mangaian theogony; Vatea is the Hawaiian Wakea.

passages.text: The universe of these islanders is to be conceived of as the hollow of a vast cocoa-nut shell. The interior of this imaginary shell is named Avaiki; at the top is a single aperture communicating with the upper world, where mortals live; at various depths are different floorings, or lands, communicating with each other. But at the very bottom of this supposed cocoa-nut shell is a thick stem, gradually tapering to a point, which represents the very beginning of all things; this point is a spirit or demon, without human form, and is named Te-aka-ia-Roe, the Root of all Existence. Above this extreme point is Te-tangaengae, or Te-vaerua - Breathing, or Life; but the thickest part of the stem is Te-manava-roa, the Long-lived, the third and last of the primary, ever-stationary, sentient spirits, who themselves constitute the foundation, and insure the permanence and well-being of all the rest of the universe.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 1 (1876); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the lowest depth of Avaiki, where the sides of the imaginary shell nearly meet, lives a woman - a demon, of flesh and blood - named Vari-ma-te-takere, the Very-beginning. Such is the narrowness of her territory that her knees and chin touch, no other position being possible. Vari-ma-te-takere was very anxious for progeny. One day she plucked off a bit of her right side, and it became a human being - the first man Avatea, or Vatea, the father of gods and men, half man and half fish, the division being like the two halves of the human body; thus one eye of Vatea was human, the other a fish-eye; his right side was furnished with an arm, the left with a fin; he had one proper foot, and half a fish-tail. But there is another, and probably far more ancient, account of Vatea, which means moon in all the dialects of Eastern Polynesia: Vatea is a man possessed of two magnificent eyes, rarely visible at the same time - whilst one, called by mortals the sun, is seen in this upper world, the other eye, called by men the moon, shines in Avaiki.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 1 (1876); not verbatim.

passages.text: The land assigned by the Great Mother to Vatea was Te-papa-rairai, the thin land - the bright land of Vatea, implying the perfect contrast between the brightness of noon-day and the utter gloom of Po. On another occasion Vari-ma-te-takere tore off a second bit from that same right side, and it became Tinirau, Innumerable, who, like his brother, had a second and fishy form; the Great Mother gave him the land of Motu-Tapu, the Sacred Isle, where were his celebrated ponds full of all kinds of fish - Tinirau was lord of the finny inhabitants of the sea, from the shark downwards. Another day Vari took a bit off her left side, and it became Tango, Support, who went to live at Enua-Kura, the land of red parrot-feathers. A fourth child was Tumuteanaoa, Echo, whose home was Te-parai-tea, the hollow grey rocks; Echo is represented as a female.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 1 (1876); not verbatim.

passages.text: A fifth child was Raka, Trouble, who presides, like Aeolus, over the winds; Raka found a congenial home in Moana-Irakau, Deep-ocean, and received from Vari a great basket in which the winds were hidden, also the knowledge of many useful inventions; the children of Raka are the numerous winds and storms which distress mankind, and to each child is allotted a hole at the edge of the horizon through which he blows at pleasure. Vari, finding that her left side had been more injured than her right, resolved to make both sides alike by taking a third bit from the right side, and named this, her last child, Tu-metua, Stick-by-the-parent, who lives with the Great Mother in that narrow strip of territory constituting the very bottom of Avaiki, the mute land, where the only language known is that of signs - such as nods, elevated eye-brows, grimaces, and smiles.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 1 (1876); not verbatim.

title.en: Maui Wins the Fire-god's Secret in the Shades

region.zh: 曼加亞冥界阿瓦伊基（象徵性定位）

source.work: W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 4, The Exploits of Maui: The Fire-god's Secret (London 1876)

summary.en: Peeping into his mother Buataranga's basket, Maui finds cooked food - the secret of fire lies in Avaiki. Borrowing Tane's red pigeon Fearless, he speaks the chasm-opening charm his mother taught him and descends into the shades, where the fire-god Mauike hurls him higher than any coconut tree - and is caught like a ball. Tortured in mid-air, Mauike bargains for life: the fire-sticks oronga and especially the banyan, and the friction-song. Maui sets all nether-world aflame, rescues the pigeon's tail, and returns to the upper world with the two fire-sticks of Mauike.
summary.zh: 毛伊偷窺母親布瓦塔蘭嘎的食籃，發現熟食——火的秘密在冥界。他借得塔內的紅鴿『無畏』，誦母親所授的裂石咒，自岩隙降入幽冥。火神毛伊凱接連將他拋向高空——高過任何椰子樹——他卻如球般被接住；精疲力竭的火神討饒求活，吐露火之奧秘：奧龍伽木、尤以榕木為要，與鑽木咒歌。毛伊縱火燒盡冥界，修復鴿尾，攜火種兩枚重返陽世。

sensitivity.note: Fire-theft cluster: Mangaian Maui descends to the shades for fire.

passages.text: Originally fire was unknown to the inhabitants of this world, who of necessity ate raw food. In nether-world (Avaiki) lived four mighty ones: Mauike, god of fire; the Sun-god Ra; Ru, supporter of the heavens; and lastly, his wife Buataranga, guardian of the road to the invisible world. To Ru and Buataranga was born a famous son, Maui. At an early age Maui was appointed one of the guardians of this upper world where mortals live. The mother occasionally visited her son, but always ate her food apart, out of a basket brought with her from nether-land. One day, when she was asleep, Maui peeped into her basket and discovered cooked food; upon tasting it he was decidedly of opinion that it was a great improvement upon the raw diet to which he was accustomed. This food came from nether-world; it was evident that the secret of fire was there. To nether-world, the home of his parents, he would descend to gain this knowledge, so that ever after he might enjoy the luxury of cooked food.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 4 (1876); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the following day Buataranga was about to descend to Avaiki, when Maui followed her through the bush without her knowing it, peering through the tall reeds, and saw his mother standing opposite a black rock, which she addressed with the magic words: 'Buataranga, descend thou bodily through this chasm. The rainbow-like must be obeyed. As two dark clouds parting at dawn: Open, open up my road to nether-world, ye fierce ones.' At these words the rock divided, and Buataranga descended. Maui carefully treasured up these magic words; and without delay started off to see the god Tane, the owner of some wonderful pigeons. Nothing would content Maui but the possession of Akaotu, Fearless, a red pigeon specially prized by Tane; Tane, who was loth to part from his pet, extracted a promise from Maui that the pigeon should be restored uninjured. Maui set off carrying the red pigeon, pronounced the magic words, and to his great delight the rock opened; entering the pigeon, he descended. Some assert that Maui transformed himself into a small dragon-fly and perched upon the back of the pigeon. The two fierce guardian demons of the chasm made a grab at the pigeon intending to devour it, but only succeeded in getting possession of the tail, whilst the pigeon, minus its beautiful tail, pursued its flight to the shades.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 4 (1876); not verbatim.

passages.text: Arrived at nether-land, Maui sought the home of his mother, guided by the sound of her cloth-flail. The red pigeon alighted on an oven-house opposite the open shed where Buataranga was beating out cloth; she guessed the red pigeon to be a visitor from the upper world, as none of the pigeons in the shades were red. 'Are you not come from daylight?' The pigeon nodded assent. 'Are you not my son Maui?' Again the pigeon nodded. Maui resumed his proper human form and went to embrace his mother, avowing that he had come to learn the secret of fire. Buataranga said the secret rested with the fire-god Mauike, whose dwelling was called Are-aoa, house-of-banyan-sticks; she entreated Maui to be careful, for the fire-god is a terrible fellow of a very irritable temper. Maui walked up boldly to the house of the fire-god and demanded a fire-brand, extinguished it in the stream, returned, and extinguished a second and a third; the fourth time Mauike was beside himself with rage, and ordered him away under pain of being tossed into the air. But the visitor said he should enjoy nothing better than a trial of strength with the fire-god.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 4 (1876); not verbatim.

passages.text: Mauike boldly seized him with both hands and hurled him to the height of a cocoa-nut tree; Maui contrived in falling to make himself so light that he was in no degree hurt. Maddened that his adversary should yet breathe, Mauike next hurled him far higher than the highest cocoa-nut tree that ever grew; yet Maui was uninjured, whilst the fire-god lay panting for breath. It was now Maui's turn: seizing the fire-god he threw him up to a dizzy height and caught him again like a ball with his hands, without allowing Mauike to touch the ground. Assured that this was but preparation for a final toss which would seal his fate, the panting and thoroughly exhausted Mauike entreated Maui to stop and to spare his life. Maui said, 'Only on one condition will I spare you: tell me the secret of fire. Where is it hidden? How is it produced?' Mauike gladly promised to tell all he knew, and led him inside his wonderful dwelling, where bundles of fire-yielding sticks - the oronga and particularly the aoa, the banyan tree - were all dry and ready for use; two smaller sticks lay by themselves, and as the fire-god plied one on the other he sang his fire-song: 'Grant, oh grant me thy hidden fire, thou banyan tree! Perform an incantation; utter a prayer to the spirit of the banyan tree! Kindle a fire for Mauike of the dust of the banyan tree!' By the time this song was completed Maui to his great joy perceived a faint smoke arising out of the fine dust produced by the friction of one stick upon another, a slight flame arose, and the grand secret of fire was secured. But the victor resolved to be revenged by setting fire to his fallen adversary's abode; in a short time all nether-world was in flames, which consumed the fire-god and all he possessed - even the rocks cracked and split with the heat: hence the ancient saying, 'The rocks at Orovaru are burning.' Ere leaving the land of ghosts Maui carefully picked up the two fire-sticks, restored the tail of the pigeon to avoid the anger of Tane, and once more pronouncing the words he learnt from Buataranga, got safely back to this upper world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 4 (1876); not verbatim.

title.en: Miru's Shades: The Bua Tree and the Fatal Net
title.zh: 米露冥府：巨樹與奪魂之網

region.zh: 曼加亞奧拉卡裂谷（象徵性定位）

source.work: W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 8, Hades; or, The Doctrine of Spirit-world (London 1876)

summary.en: Avaiki, the hollow under Mangaia, is reached at death by a leaping-place of souls facing the setting sun. A gigantic bua tree springs up from the shades to receive the spirit, with a branch for each clan; at the foot Akaanga spreads the net of innumerable meshes, and the drowned ghosts are dragged before the ruddy Miru, who feeds her visitors on red earth-worms and black beetles, stews them in her ever-burning oven. Warriors slain in battle escape her - only women, cowards and children are annihilated.
summary.zh: 阿瓦伊基——曼加亞之下的空洞——亡魂自面西的『魂躍之地』一躍而下。冥土升起一株巨大布瓦樹，枝幹各歸各族；樹底阿卡安加張開『千孔之網』，溺魂被拖至紅面米露前：以紅蚯蚓與黑甲蟲飼之，置於永不熄滅之灶蒸煮。唯戰場陣亡的武士得免——婦孺與懦夫皆被吞滅。

sensitivity.note: Death-eschatology record; the spirit's road closed by Tiki noted in passages.

passages.text: The proper name for Hades is Avaiki; in Tahitian, Hawaii; in New Zealand, Hawaiki. As the dead were usually thrown down the deepest chasms, it was not unnatural for their friends to imagine the earth to be hollow, and the entrance to this vast nether-world to be down one of these pits: the outer portion of Mangaia is a honeycomb, the rock being pierced in every direction with winding caves and frightful chasms. The inland opening to this subterranean territory was the grand repository of the dead, and is known by the significant name of Auraka - murder; doubtless this is the true origin of their idea of the whereabouts of spirit-world. The proper denizens of Avaiki are the major and lesser divinities with their dependants; these marry, multiply, and quarrel like mortals; they wear clothing, plant, cook, fish, build, and inhabit dwellings of exactly the same sort as exist on earth. The visible world itself is but a gross copy of what exists in spirit-land: if fire burns, it is because latent flame was hidden in the wood by Mauike in Hades.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 8 (1876); not verbatim.

passages.text: The high-road to Avaiki is for ever closed; this was not the fault of mankind, but the penalty of the excesses of the denizens of spirit-land. They became very troublesome to mankind - continually afflicting them with disease and death; they occasioned great dearth by stealing all kinds of food, and even ravished the women of this world. The brave and beautiful Tiki, the sister of Veetini, determined to put an end to these annoyances; for this purpose she rolled herself alive down into the gloomy opening, which immediately closed upon her. From that memorable day the spirits of mortals have been compelled to descend to Avaiki by a different route; happily, however, the natives of Avaiki no longer dare molest mankind, and the closed chasm is known by the name of Tiki's hole.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 8 (1876); not verbatim.

passages.text: The point of departure for spirit-land is called a reinga vaerua; there are three on Mangaia, all facing the setting sun. The standard and esoteric teaching of the priests was that the souls of the dying leave the body ere breath is quite extinct, and travel to the edge of the cliff at Araia near the marae of Rongo, facing the west. If a friendly spirit should meet the solitary wanderer at any point of the sad but inevitable journey and should say, 'Go back and live', the now joyful ghost at once returns to its old home and re-inhabits the once forsaken body - this is the native theory of fainting. But if no friendly spirit interfere, the departing soul pursues its mournful travels and eventually reaches the extreme edge of the cliff. Instantly a large wave approaches to the base, and at the same moment a gigantic bua tree, covered with fragrant blossom, springs up from Avaiki to receive on its far-reaching branches unhappy human spirits; even at this last moment a friendly voice may send the spirit-traveller back to life and health. Otherwise he is mysteriously impelled to climb the particular branch reserved for his own tribe and conveniently brought nearest to him: the worshippers of Motoro have a branch to themselves, the worshippers of Tane have another - the tree having just as many branches as there are principal gods in Mangaia.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 8 (1876); not verbatim.

passages.text: Immediately the human soul is safely lodged upon this gigantic tree, the bua goes down with its living burden to nether-world; while yet on the tree the wretched spirit looks down to the root, and to his horror sees a great net spread out beneath to catch it - hence the proverb in regard to the dying, 'Will be caught in the net of innumerable meshes', the net of Akaanga. This net, from the strong meshes of which there is no escape, is firmly held by Akaanga and his assistants; the doomed spirit at last falls into this fatal net, and is at once submerged in a lake of fresh water near the foot of the gigantic bua tree, named Vai-roto-ariki, the royal fresh-water lake; in these treacherous waters captive ghosts exhaust themselves by wriggling like fishes in the vain hope of escape. The great net is eventually pulled up, and the half-drowned spirits tremblingly enter the presence of the inexpressibly ugly Miru, generally called the ruddy, because her face reflects the glowing heat of her ever-burning oven. The hag feeds her unwilling visitors with red earth-worms, black beetles, crabs, and small blackbirds. The grand secret of Miru's power over her intended victims is the kava root, one vast root named by her Tevoo, her own peculiar property; her four lovely daughters are directed to prepare bowls of this strong kava for her unwilling visitors. Utterly stupefied with the draught, the unresisting victims are borne off to the oven and cooked; Miru, with her son and peerless daughters, subsist on these human spirits. Such is the inevitable fate of those who die a natural death - that is, of women, cowards, and children; they are annihilated. Not so warriors slain on the field of battle: the spirits of these lucky fellows for a while wander about amongst the rocks and trees in the neighbourhood of which their bodies were thrown.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 8 (1876); not verbatim.

title.en: Veetini, the First to Die, Returns on the Sun's Path
title.zh: 首位逝者維蒂尼循日路歸來

region.zh: 曼加亞蘭吉卡普阿山丘

source.work: W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 9, Veetini; or, The Immortality of the Soul (London 1876)

summary.en: Veetini, first to die a natural death in Mangaia, is mourned with the dirge, funeral games and black pakoko garments invented for him. His spirit returns once along the sun's golden path, granted a detained sun by great Tangaroa to converse with his parents at a booth on Karanga-iti, teaches mortals the food-offerings for the dead, and at Vairorongo, Rongo's sacred stream, shouts 'Thrust down the sun, that I may descend to nether-land' - grasped at, he is only a shadow, and vanishes forever in the train of the setting sun.
summary.zh: 維蒂尼——曼加亞首位自然死亡者——其親人為之創制輓歌、喪舞與染黑的帕科科喪服。其魂循太陽的金色軌跡一度歸來：經坦加羅亞恩准，太陽為之停留，他在卡拉恩加伊提的涼棚下與父母敘談，教世人以食物祭亡者；至瓦伊羅龍戈——龍戈聖溪——他高呼『沉下太陽，我好下降冥府』。父母伸手挽留，抓住的只是影子；他隨落日金光，永逝而去。

sensitivity.note: Origin-legend of Mangaian funeral rites and food-offerings to the dead.

passages.text: The first who ever died a natural death in Mangaia was Veetini. He was the only and much beloved son of Tueva and his wife Manga. But Veetini, when in the prime of early manhood, sickened and died. The parents, in their grief, instituted those signs of mourning and funeral games which were ever afterwards observed amongst these islanders. The chief mourners were Tueva, Manga, and the lovely Tiki, the attached sister of Veetini. All these, with the more distant relatives, blackened their faces, cut off their hair, slashed their bodies with shark's teeth, and wore only pakoko, or native cloth, dyed red in the sap of the candle-nut tree and then dipped in the black mud of a taro-patch - the very offensive smell of this mourning garment is symbolical of the putrescent state of the dead. It was on account of Veetini that the eva, or dirge, in its four varieties, and the mourning dance, were invented and performed by the sorrowing relatives day by day. During the entire period of mourning no beating of bark for native cloth was permitted in the district where the death occurred, to avoid giving offence to the female demon Mueu, who introduced cloth-beating to this world, but who herself beats out cloth of a very different texture: her cloth-flail is the stroke of death - hence the proverb when a person dies, 'Ah! Mueu's flail is once more at work!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 9 (1876); not verbatim.

passages.text: The last resting-place of Veetini is at Rangikapua, a green spot about half a mile from the sea, a hill about 100 feet above the level of the ocean, on which the rays of the setting sun fall. On the evening he was buried the dirges and dances that had been invented in his honour were performed, and the parents and the sister looked wistfully towards the north, hoping for his return to their midst - but in vain! The mourning band walked in sad procession along the western shore, chanting dirges; they sought the lost one on the southern and almost inaccessible shore of Mangaia, and at last arrived at the eastern coast, gazing over the vast expanse swept by the life-giving trade-winds. At night they occupied the Ruddy Cave, Ana-kura, its entrance washed by the surf. Ere dawn Tueva rose from his stony couch to watch the rising of the sun; as it rose in all its wonted glory he noticed a tiny dark speck beneath on the ocean, which grew larger and drew nearer, passing over the ocean in the bright trail of the sun - on arriving nearer still, this wonderful object, lightly skimming over the crest of the waves, proved to be no other than their own lost Veetini!
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 9 (1876); not verbatim.

passages.text: The now rejoicing parents rushed forwards to kiss their son, who was indeed Veetini, yet not altogether like his former self. He said to the joyful throng that he had been permitted to revisit this upper world in consequence of the passionate lamentations of his parents, and to comfort their sorrowing hearts; he also came to show mortals how to make offerings of food to please the dead. For himself, he had come and must depart in the bright track of the sun, being now a denizen of spirit-land. However, to gratify his parents and friends, Veetini asked great Tangaroa to detain the sun for a short time in its course, in order that he might rest and converse awhile with his relatives; the prayer was granted, and the sun was detained while Veetini and his friends pleasantly rested in a sort of extempore house erected for him on the spot known as Karanga-iti.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 9 (1876); not verbatim.

passages.text: At length Veetini rose, and led the half-glad and half-sorrowful procession along the beach towards the west; at last they reached Vairorongo, Rongo's sacred stream, directly facing the setting sun. Here they rested a few minutes only, as day was fast fading away. As the sun disappeared beneath the horizon Veetini said he must go; the weeping parents begged him to stay with them. The son replied, 'I cannot; I do not belong to this world now', and then shouted impatiently: 'Thrust down the sun, that I may descend to nether-land!' The parents now endeavoured to detain him by force; but lo! they grasped at a shadow. They watched him gliding swiftly over the western ocean in the ruddy track of the sun, and, with its last rays, Veetini, now a tiny distant speck in the train of the king of day, for ever disappeared.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 9 (1876); not verbatim.

title.en: The Ghost Train That Follows the Setting Sun
title.zh: 隨落日西行的幽魂列車

region.en: Ana-kura red cave and reinga, Mangaia
region.zh: 曼加亞紅洞與魂躍之地

source.work: W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 8 (London 1876)

summary.en: Mangaian ghosts wander the shore in ghostly net-work and turbaned red twine, most delighted to follow the sun. They muster at the red cave Ana-kura or at Karanga-iti, dance and revisit old homes, and when their leader gives the word, flit along the coast to Vairorongo and, at sunset, enter Avaiki through the very aperture by which the Sun-god descends - 'Tis night now in spirit-land; for 'tis light in this upper world.' A laggard must wait a whole season, dancing the dance of the starved.
summary.zh: 曼加亞幽魂披幽網、纏紅繩，沿濱流浪，最喜追隨太陽。它們聚於紅洞阿納庫拉或小迎地卡拉恩加伊提，歌舞盤桓、重訪舊居；待首領一聲令下，便沿海岸飄至瓦伊羅龍戈，日落時分循日神下冥之口而入——『此刻冥府正夜；而陽世正晝。』落伍的孤魂則須苦候一季，跳『餓鬼之舞』消磨光陰。

passages.text: The spirits of the dead were often spoken of as wandering along the margin of the sea most disconsolately, not a little annoyed at the extreme sharpness of the rocks, and the entanglement of their feet in the bindweed and thick vines. They were arrayed in ghostly net-work, and a fantastic mourning of weeds picked upon the way, relieved, however, by the fragrant heliotrope which grows freely on the barren rocks; a red creeper, resembling dyed twine, wound round and round the head like a turban, completed their ghostly toilet. Rather inconsistently with this, a smooth, shelving piece of coral rock on the western coast is known as 'the place where ghosts blanch their new-made garments', as if during the weary months of their wanderings they were driven, like the living, to prepare new clothing from time to time. The great delight of these weeping, melancholy spirits was to follow the sun: at the summer solstice, January, he apparently rises out of the ocean opposite to Ana-kura, the red-cave; at the winter solstice, June, rising at Karanga-iti. These points became, therefore, grand rendezvous of disembodied spirits: those belonging to the northern half of the island assembling at the last-named rendezvous, those belonging to the southern half meeting at the former.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 8 (1876); not verbatim.

passages.text: Many months might elapse ere the projected departure of the ghosts took place. This weary interval was spent in dances and in revisiting their former homes, where the living dwell affectionately remembered by the dead; at night-fall they would wander amongst the trees and plantations nearest to these dwellings, sometimes venturing to peep inside. As a rule these ghosts were well-disposed to their own living relatives, but often became vindictive if a pet child was ill-treated by a step-mother or other relatives. Sometimes wearied with these wanderings, the ghosts huddled together in the Red-cave, or clambered up the open lawn-like place above it - now a favourite resting-place for fishermen - known as One-ma-kenu-kenu, the smooth spot. The precise period for final departure was fixed by the leader of the band; but if no distinguished person was amongst them, they must of course wait until such a leader was obtained; thus in the classic laments for Vera, he is represented as the chosen captain of the dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 8 (1876); not verbatim.

passages.text: The chief of this disconsolate throng resolves to depart; messages are sent to collect those stray ghosts who may yet be lingering near their ancient haunts. With many tears and last lingering looks they assemble at the Red-cave, intently watching the rising of the sun. At the first streak of dawn the entire band take their departure to meet the rising sun; this done, they follow in his train as nearly as may be - he in the heavens above, they at first on the ocean beneath, but afterwards over the rocks and stones, always avoiding the interior of the island - until late in the afternoon of the appointed day they are all assembled at Vairorongo, facing the setting sun.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 8 (1876); not verbatim.

passages.text: At last the congregated throng, whose eyes are fixed upon the setting sun, feel that the moment has come when they must for ever depart from the cherished scenes of earth, despite the tears and solicitations of relatives, who are frequently represented as chasing their loved ones over rocks and across fearful precipices round half the island. The sun now sinks in the ocean, leaving a golden track; the entire band of ghosts take a last farewell, and, following their earthly leader, flit over the ocean in the train of the Sun-god Ra, but not like him destined to reappear on the morrow; the ghostly train enter Avaiki through the very aperture by which the Sun-god descends in order to lighten up for a time those dark subterranean regions - as the priest Teka sang in 1794: 'Tis night now in spirit-land; for 'tis light in this upper world.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 8 (1876); not verbatim.

title.en: Five Nuts for the Dead: Offerings Taught by Veetini
title.zh: 亡者五椰：維蒂尼所授祭食

region.zh: 曼加亞墳塋（象徵性定位）

source.work: W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 9, Veetini Meeting His Father (London 1876)

summary.en: 'I came to instruct you in making food-offerings to the dead,' said Veetini to his weeping father. From that teaching came the rite: five old coconuts opened and poured out in turn, wrapped in leaves and cloth and thrown towards the grave - or down the chasm of Auraka - each time the name of the departed called loudly, 'Here is thy food; eat it'; and at the fifth, 'Farewell! we come back no more to thee!'
summary.zh: 維蒂尼對泣父言：『我來教你祭奠亡者之法。』由此傳下祭禮：依次開啟五枚老椰，傾汁於地，以葉布裹之擲向墳塋——或拋入奧拉卡深谷——每次高呼亡者之名：『此乃你的食物，吃吧！』至第五枚並布丁擲下，則道：『別了！我們不再來看你！』

sensitivity.note: Funeral-rite origin; includes Gill's later anecdote of the last heathen mourner Arikikaka.

passages.text: Tueva, who seven times lamented for his boy, asked, 'Why didst thou return to this world?' 'I came', said Veetini, 'to instruct you in making food-offerings to the dead: offerings to those in spirit-world; gifts from their relatives who yet linger in this upper world.' Such was the belief and practice of heathenism. As soon as the corpse was committed to its last resting-place, the mourners selected five old cocoa-nuts, which were successively opened, and the water poured out upon the ground; these nuts were then wrapped up in leaves and native cloth, and thrown towards the grave; or, if the corpse were let down with cords into the deep chasm of Auraka, the nuts and other food would be successively thrown down upon it. Calling loudly each time the name of the departed, they said, 'Here is thy food; eat it.' When the fifth nut and the accompanying raroi, or pudding, were thrown down, the mourners said, 'Farewell! we come back no more to thee!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 9 (1876); not verbatim.

passages.text: Seventeen years before Gill wrote, Arikikaka, the last heathen of Mangaia, lost his only son, a consistent church member; the old man was inconsolable. The corpse was buried with his mother's deceased relatives on the west of the island, and the friends dispersed to their respective homes. A day or two after, Arikikaka and his wife walked with difficulty across the island, arriving at dusk at the grave of their beloved son with a basket of cooked food and some unopened cocoa-nuts; with many tears and affectionate words they called upon their boy to eat the food and drink the nuts - carefully opened for the convenience of the ghost at the grave, the contents poured out upon the earth - which they had carried six miles. The aged couple slept under a tree close to the last resting-place of their son, and at dawn on the following morning departed. Gill adds that in May, 1865, Arikikaka and his wife were baptized - 'at eventime there was light.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 9 (1876); not verbatim.

title.en: Tinirau, Innumerable, Lord of the Fish

region.en: Motu-Tapu, the Sacred Isle, Avaiki (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿瓦伊基聖島莫圖塔普（象徵性定位）

source.work: W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 1 (London 1876)

summary.en: Torn from Vari's right side as her second son, Tinirau - Innumerable - is half man, half sprat, with fish-ponds at the Sacred Isle teeming with every fin from shark downwards. He is the father of the Tinirau cycle: the fish-ponds that draw Ina, the pet whale ridden by Kae, the ten daughters - a divine ancestor whose name the Maori south-sea traditions share.
summary.zh: 自瓦里右側撕下的第二子蒂尼勞——『無數者』——半人半鯡，聖島上池塘魚群自鯊以下無所不有。他是蒂尼勞傳說之祖：引伊娜前來的魚塘、被凱竊騎的寵鯨、眾多女兒——其名亦見於毛利與南方海域傳統。

sensitivity.note: Divine genealogy record connecting to the Kae/whale cycle.

passages.text: On another occasion Vari-ma-te-takere tore off a second bit from that same right side, and it became Tinirau, Innumerable, who, like his brother, had a second and fishy form; the sort of fish which composed his half fish body was of the sprat-kind. The Great Mother gave him the land of Motu-Tapu, the Sacred Isle, as his own domain; there were his celebrated ponds full of all kinds of fish, and Tinirau was lord of the finny inhabitants of the sea, from the shark downwards.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 1 (1876); not verbatim.

passages.text: At Ngatangiia, Rarotonga, there is an islet, covered with cocoa-nut trees, so named Motu Tapu - this is, of course, a modern identification; the Sacred Isle is supposed to be in the shades. Tinirau became in later myth the father of the great Tinirau cycle of the south seas - the lord of the fish-ponds to which the fairy voyager Ina was carried, the owner of the pet whale which Kae rode and destroyed, and the father of the many daughters sung in the day-songs of Mangaia.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 1 (1876); not verbatim.
